narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your plan to attend law school part-time rather than full-time was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction noticeably toward failure. Among students who were accepted, 93% planned to study full-time; only 7% were part-time. Your choice placed you in that small group, and the model sees part-time study as a meaningful risk for first-time bar success.

Second, your undergraduate GPA of 2.40 was well below the 3.23 average of accepted students. This lower academic performance also pulled the prediction toward failure, though less strongly than your part-time status.

Third, your family income being in the upper-middle bracket actually worked slightly in your favor, nudging the outcome a little toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other two factors.

In short, the combination of part-time enrollment plans and a lower college GPA created enough concern about bar exam readiness that the model could not confidently recommend admission.

What you should do next is consider reapplying after improving your academic record—perhaps by taking additional coursework to raise your GPA—or by committing to full-time study. Either change could meaningfully improve your chances in a future application. (218 words)
